1311.event_title: The Beatles appear on The Ed Sullivan Show
1311.event: On the evening of 9 February 1964 the Beatles made their debut on the CBS programme The Ed Sullivan Show. About 73 million people tuned in, and the band played to a studio audience filled with screaming teenage fans. The appearance helped spread the craze that British newspapers had already named Beatlemania across the United States.
1311.explanation: It is one of the best-documented moments when millions of admirers fixed their eyes on the same few performers at once, a kind of shared adoration that television made possible.
1311.tie_back: The wife in this kural refuses to come near a man whom every woman already gazes at as if he belonged to all, and the screaming crowds of 1964 show what that kind of shared, public admiration looks like.
1311._accuracy_note: The event shows mass admiration of men by many women, but it has no jealous partner who keeps away, so it only illustrates half of the kural's picture.

1312.event_title: Fred Ott sneezes for Edison's camera
1312.event: When a journalist from Harper's Weekly asked Thomas Edison's laboratory for someone to perform a sneeze for the Kinetograph camera, the mechanic Fred Ott agreed. W. K. L. Dickson and William Heise filmed his sneeze in the first week of January 1894, and the record was deposited for copyright at the Library of Congress on 9 January 1894 as Edison Kinetoscopic Record of a Sneeze. It became one of the most famous early motion pictures.
1312.explanation: The sneeze was performed on purpose, at a request, so that it would be seen and noticed, which made an ordinary bodily act into a famous piece of film history.
1312.tie_back: In the kural the husband sneezes on purpose, knowing it will force his sulking wife to speak, and Fred Ott's sneeze is a documented case of a sneeze made deliberately to get a reaction.
1312._accuracy_note: Only the idea of a deliberate sneeze carries over; there is no sulking partner and no custom of blessing, so this is a next-best example.

1313.event_title: Othello, the play of the misread handkerchief, is staged at court
1313.event: William Shakespeare wrote Othello in about 1603 to 1604. The Revels accounts for 1604 to 1605 record a performance of the Moor of Venis by the King's Men at the court of King James I, one of the earliest records of the play. In the story the villain Iago uses a handkerchief that Desdemona has innocently lost to persuade her husband Othello that she has given it to another man as a love token.
1313.explanation: The play became one of the most famous studies of jealousy in world literature because it shows how an innocent object can be twisted into false proof of love for someone else.
1313.tie_back: Like the wife in this kural who decides that a simple garland must have been worn to impress another woman, Othello reads an innocent handkerchief as a sign meant for a rival.
1313._accuracy_note: The play captures the kural's idea of an innocent object misread as aimed at a rival, though Othello's jealousy is tragic rather than the playful sulk of the kural.

1314.event_title: One clause of the Treaty of Wichale is read two different ways
1314.event: On 2 May 1889 Emperor Menilek II of Ethiopia signed a treaty of friendship and commerce with Italy at Wichale. The Italian text of Article XVII made Rome the channel for all of Ethiopia's foreign relations, while the Amharic text was only permissive, saying Ethiopia could use Italy's help if it wished. Italy used the Italian wording to claim a protectorate over Ethiopia, Menilek rejected that reading, and the treaty was finally cancelled by the Treaty of Addis Ababa in October 1896.
1314.explanation: The episode is a classic example of how a small difference in wording can be read as implying something the other side never meant, with very large consequences.
1314.tie_back: In this kural the wife seizes on the word than anyone and reads into it a list of rivals the husband never had in mind, just as one side at Wichale read a much bigger meaning into a single clause.
1314._accuracy_note: It shares the kural's mechanism of a phrase pressed for an implication it did not have, but it is a diplomatic dispute, not a lovers' quarrel.

1315.event_title: Etruscan artists make the Sarcophagus of the Spouses
1315.event: In the Etruscan city of Cerveteri, artists modelled a nearly life-size terracotta sarcophagus showing a husband and wife reclining side by side on a banqueting couch, close and affectionate, as if sharing a meal. The work, now in the Louvre, has a nearly identical companion in the Villa Giulia museum in Rome, which was discovered near Cerveteri on 9 April 1881. Scholars note that the figures may once have held objects for the journey from this life to the next.
1315.explanation: The sarcophagus is one of the best-known ancient images of a married couple who expected to stay together beyond death.
1315.tie_back: The wife in this kural weeps because she hears in never part in this life a hint that they might part in the next, and the Etruscan couple show the opposite hope, of being together after this life too.
1315._accuracy_note: It illustrates the belief in lovers staying together across lives that the kural assumes, but it does not show the misunderstanding that is the kural's point.

1316.event_title: William Jones publishes Sacontala, or The Fatal Ring
1316.event: In 1789 Sir William Jones published in Calcutta an English translation of Kalidasa's Sanskrit and Prakrit drama Shakuntala under the title Sacontala; or, The Fatal Ring. The play's Sanskrit title means Shakuntala recalled through recognition, and it turns on a king who must be brought to remember his wife with the help of a ring. Jones's translation was soon reprinted in London and Edinburgh and became widely influential in Europe.
1316.explanation: The translation introduced Europe to one of the great love dramas of India, a story built around forgetting and remembering a beloved.
1316.tie_back: The wife in this kural turns I remembered you into So you had forgotten me, and Shakuntala is the classic Indian drama of a lover who forgets and must be made to remember.
1316._accuracy_note: The theme of remembering and forgetting a beloved matches, but the play's forgetting is real and serious rather than an innocent word misread, so the fit is partial.

1317.event_title: Murasaki Shikibu writes The Tale of Genji
1317.event: Murasaki Shikibu, a lady serving at the Japanese imperial court, wrote The Tale of Genji in the early eleventh century; her own diary shows she was writing it in 1008, and she probably completed it about 1010. Most of its 54 chapters concern the loves of the handsome courtier Genji, and each of the women in his life is drawn with great sensitivity. It is often called the world's first novel.
1317.explanation: The work is a landmark of world literature and a detailed record of the emotional lives, including the hurt feelings and suspicions, of lovers at the Heian court.
1317.tie_back: The kural's wife first blesses her husband and then weeps, wondering which other woman is thinking of him, and Murasaki's novel is the classic early portrait of women who must share the attention of one admired man.
1317._accuracy_note: This is a next-best choice: the novel's world of shared affections fits the mood, but nothing in it matches the specific sneeze-and-suspicion scene of the kural.

1318.event_title: The Affair of the Diamond Necklace
1318.event: In 1784 and 1785 the confidence trickster Jeanne de La Motte persuaded Cardinal de Rohan that Queen Marie Antoinette secretly wanted a famous diamond necklace, arranging a night meeting with a woman who impersonated the queen. Rohan obtained the necklace on 1 February 1785 and handed it to La Motte, who disappeared with it. When the jewellers asked for payment the plot came to light, Rohan was arrested at Versailles on 15 August 1785 and acquitted by the Parlement de Paris on 31 May 1786, yet the innocent queen's reputation was badly damaged.
1318.explanation: The affair shows how a secret kept or a story hidden can make an innocent person look guilty in the eyes of others.
1318.tie_back: In this kural the husband holds back even a sneeze to avoid suspicion, only to be accused of hiding something, and Marie Antoinette, who had done nothing, was blamed all the more because the affair seemed to involve secrets.
1318._accuracy_note: The idea of an innocent person suspected of hiding something carries over, but this is a court scandal, not a tender lovers' quarrel.

1319.event_title: Franz Liszt's years of adulation end his life with Marie d'Agoult
1319.place: Europe (Paris and the Rhine island of Nonnenwerth)
1319.event: Franz Liszt and the Countess Marie d'Agoult lived together in Switzerland and Italy and had three children, but late in 1839 their relationship became strained and she returned to Paris. Liszt then spent about eight years touring Europe, where his concerts caused a sensation and he was received everywhere with great adulation. The couple still spent summers together on the Rhine island of Nonnenwerth until 1844, when their stormy relationship ended in a bitter parting.
1319.explanation: Liszt was the first great celebrity performer, and his story shows how a lover's charm for the whole world can unsettle the person closest to him.
1319.tie_back: The wife in this kural cannot enjoy her husband's coaxing because she thinks he must charm other women the same way, and Marie d'Agoult watched Liszt's charm win over audiences across Europe before their relationship broke apart.
1319._accuracy_note: Liszt's public charm and the strain it put on his partner fit the kural's suspicion well, though the sources do not record the specific complaint the kural describes.

1320.event_title: Rossetti paints his wife as Dante's Beatrice in Beata Beatrix
1320.event: Dante Gabriel Rossetti married his model Elizabeth Siddal in 1860, and she died in 1862. In the following years he painted Beata Beatrix, now in Tate Britain, in which a figure based on his late wife represents Beatrice, the beloved of the poet Dante, in a dreamlike trance. Britannica notes that the painting shows he saw his love for his wife as like Dante's idealised love for Beatrice.
1320.explanation: The painting is a famous example of an artist gazing at his own wife's features while thinking of a woman from literature.
1320.tie_back: The wife in this kural asks whom her husband is thinking of while he gazes at her, and in Beata Beatrix Rossetti literally looked at his wife's face and painted another woman, Dante's Beatrice.
1320._accuracy_note: It neatly mirrors the kural's gaze that seems to have another woman in mind, though in Rossetti's case the other woman was a literary ideal and the painting was made after his wife's death.
